summaries.summary: The blessing over the Shabbat candles marks the transition from the ordinary week into sacred time. By lighting the candles before Shabbat and reciting the blessing, the home welcomes the holiness, peace, and rest of Shabbat.

Psalm 95, attributed to **King David**, opens with an invitation to sing joyfully to God and bow before the Creator and Shepherd of Israel. It then turns to warning, recalling the wilderness generation that tested God and hardened its heart. The psalm contrasts joyful worship with the danger of spiritual stubbornness: praise must lead to listening and faithfulness. Its closing words remember Israel’s forty years of wandering. Biblical citation: **Psalm 95:1–11**.

“Arbaim Shana”—“forty years”—comes from the closing section of **Psalm 95:7–11**, attributed to **King David**. It recalls the wilderness generation that repeatedly tested God after the Exodus. Their forty years of wandering become a warning against hardening the heart and refusing to recognize God’s ways. The passage shifts the psalm from joyful praise to moral challenge: worship is incomplete unless hearing God leads to trust, responsiveness, and faithfulness.

Psalm 29 is especially apt at the opening of this Rosh Hashanah Friday-evening service because its sevenfold “voice of the Lord” moves through creation with overwhelming power and ends unexpectedly in peace. Rabbinic and liturgical tradition made the psalm part of Kabbalat Shabbat; here it also supplies a fitting High Holiday soundscape of kingship, awe, and judgment. The final turn—God gives strength to the people and blesses them with peace—moves the congregation from cosmic power toward the welcome of Shabbat.

L'cha Dodi was written by Shlomo ha-Levi Alkabetz (c. 1505-1584), a kabbalist and poet of 16th-century Safed. The first letters of its first eight stanzas spell his name, Shlomo HaLevi. The poem grew out of the Safed practice of welcoming Shabbat as bride and queen, but it repeatedly shifts from Shabbat to Jerusalem, exile, and redemption, so welcoming Shabbat becomes a rehearsal for national restoration. De Sola Pool's Sabbath Prayer Book has the congregation stand for the final stanza, preserving the poem as ritual action, not just song.

Kaddish deRabbanan is an **Aramaic** form of Kaddish associated with Torah study and rabbinic teaching. In addition to magnifying God’s name, it asks for peace, grace, lovingkindness, and compassion upon Israel, the rabbis, their students, and all who engage in Torah. Its distinctive emphasis is the community of learning: study is treated not merely as intellectual activity but as sacred work deserving protection, blessing, and peace.

Psalm 92 is the biblical “song for the Sabbath day,” making it the natural scriptural declaration that Shabbat has arrived even on Rosh Hashanah. Its contrast between the temporary flourishing of the wicked and the enduring rootedness of the righteous gives the psalm a second resonance on a Day of Judgment. The righteous “flourish like the palm tree” and remain fruitful in old age: Shabbat rest is framed not as withdrawal, but as confidence that moral order outlasts immediate appearances.

Kaddish is an **Aramaic** doxology magnifying and sanctifying God’s name and praying for divine sovereignty, redemption, life, and peace. Its central congregational response—“May His great name be blessed forever and ever”—became one of Jewish prayer’s most recognizable affirmations. The prayer contains no confession and little direct petition for the individual; its focus is the greatness of God and the hope that divine peace and wholeness will become manifest in the world.

Barchu is not simply another line of praise: it is the formal summons that begins the public evening prayer sequence. Leader and congregation answer one another, making its communal character essential. In this Rosh Hashanah service it follows the introductory Shabbat and New Year material and announces that the service is entering the blessings surrounding the Shema. The High Holiday melody can make a very short text carry the atmosphere of the season before the words themselves become specifically seasonal.

Maariv Aravim treats nightfall as an act of creation renewed every evening: God changes times, orders the stars, and alternates light and darkness. On Rosh Hashanah evening that daily theology acquires unusual force. The congregation is not only watching one day become night but entering a new year. The blessing deliberately remains universal rather than mentioning Rosh Hashanah; the ordinary cycle of evening becomes the frame within which the extraordinary sacred day begins.

Ahavat Olam places divine love immediately before the Shema and defines that love through Torah, commandments, and covenant rather than sentiment alone. The evening rite uses Ahavat Olam—“everlasting love”—where other liturgical settings use the related Ahavah Rabbah formulation. On Rosh Hashanah this placement matters: before proclaiming God’s unity and kingship, the congregation first remembers that the relationship being judged is also a relationship grounded in enduring love and teaching.

The Shema and Ve’ahavta proclaim **God’s unity** and Israel’s covenantal responsibility. The Shema declares, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Ve’ahavta continues with the command to love God wholeheartedly, teach these words to one’s children, speak of them continually, and bind them as signs on hand, head, and doorposts (Deuteronomy 6:5–9).

Ve’ahavta, **Deuteronomy 6:5–9**, commands Israel to love God “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.” It makes covenantal loyalty a daily discipline: God’s words are to remain in the heart, be taught to children, spoken at home and on the road, bound on hand and head, and written on doorposts. The passage connects love of God with memory, education, and embodied practice.

The second paragraph of the Shema, **Deuteronomy 11:13–21**, links faithfulness to the covenant with rain, harvest, and life in the land. Israel is commanded to love and serve God, guard against idolatry, teach these words to children, and bind them as signs on hand, head, and doorposts. The passage emphasizes collective responsibility: the community’s choices have consequences, and covenantal faithfulness sustains life across generations.

The third paragraph of the Shema, **Numbers 15:37–41**, commands the Israelites to wear tzitzit as a visible reminder of God’s commandments. The fringes are meant to turn memory into action: seeing them should prompt Israel to remember and perform the mitzvot rather than follow the impulses of heart and eyes. The passage concludes by recalling the Exodus from Egypt and declaring God’s continuing claim upon Israel.

The closing words of the third paragraph of the Shema, **Numbers 15:40–41**, command Israel to remember and perform God’s commandments and to become holy. They immediately recall the Exodus: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” The passage connects freedom with obligation—Israel was liberated not simply from slavery but into covenantal responsibility. The final word, **Emet—“truth”**, links this biblical declaration to the blessing of redemption that follows.

Emet VeEmunah—“True and faithful”—praises God as the **faithful Redeemer of Israel**. It affirms the truth of the Shema, recalls deliverance from Egypt, and describes God’s saving power as consistent across generations. The prayer transforms the Exodus from ancient history into a continuing claim about divine character: the God who redeemed the ancestors remains trustworthy. Its language of truth and faithfulness prepares for the Song at the Sea and the blessing of redemption.

Mi Chamocha quotes Israel’s Song at the Sea (Exodus 15), but in the Rosh Hashanah evening service its language of incomparable divine power also anticipates the day’s central theme of kingship. The Exodus is not recalled merely as history: redemption becomes evidence that God acts in history and can redeem again. The passage moves from “Who is like You?” to divine reign and finally Ga’al Yisrael, allowing the congregation to approach the Amidah carrying both memory of past deliverance and hope for future redemption.

Hashkiveinu is the evening prayer of vulnerability: once darkness falls, the worshipper asks to lie down in peace, rise again to life, and be sheltered from danger. On Friday night its conclusion is expanded around the image of the sukkat shalom, the “shelter of peace,” linking nightly protection with Shabbat. On Rosh Hashanah falling on Friday evening, that image joins two forms of dependence at once—the vulnerability of night and the uncertainty of entering a new year under divine judgment.

Veshamru is Exodus 31:16–17, one of the Torah’s clearest descriptions of Shabbat as an enduring covenantal sign between God and Israel. Its appearance on Rosh Hashanah Friday evening is important precisely because it is not a High Holiday text: Rosh Hashanah does not displace Shabbat. The congregation simultaneously inhabits the annual drama of judgment and the weekly covenant of sacred rest, and Veshamru makes the Shabbat identity of this particular Rosh Hashanah explicit.

The Rosh Hashanah evening Amidah combines the familiar architecture of the standing prayer with the theology of the Day of Remembrance: divine kingship, judgment, memory, holiness of the festival, and hope for life. Because this Rosh Hashanah is also Shabbat, the Amidah must hold both sacred identities at once. That makes the prayer a liturgical intersection rather than simply a longer holiday Amidah: weekly creation and rest meet the annual renewal of the year before the same God addressed as both covenantal protector and King.

This concluding blessing of the Amidah asks God to establish **peace, goodness, blessing, grace, lovingkindness, and compassion** upon Israel. It gathers the prayer’s many petitions into a final vision of wholeness, asking that divine favor and blessing rest upon the people. Peace here is more than the absence of conflict: it represents completeness, security, relationship, and well-being—the conditions under which all other blessings can endure.

Elohai Netzor—“My God, guard my tongue from evil”—is a personal meditation traditionally associated with **Mar bar Ravina** in the Talmud (**Berakhot 17a**). It asks for restraint in speech, humility before hostility, openness to Torah, and protection from harmful intentions. The prayer shifts the Amidah from formal communal blessings to intensely personal moral discipline. Its central request is striking: before asking God to change others, the worshipper asks for control of one’s own words, impulses, and reactions.

“May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, O Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer” comes from **Psalm 19:15**, attributed to **King David**. The verse turns from spoken words to inner intention, asking that both be worthy before God. Its pairing of speech and thought makes it a compact statement that authentic prayer requires not only correct words but a heart aligned with them.

Oseh Shalom asks the God who “makes peace in the heavens” to bring **peace upon us and upon all Israel**. Its imagery looks to the ordered heavens as a model for harmony on earth. The prayer is closely associated with the conclusion of Kaddish and the Amidah, where it transforms praise and petition into a final hope for reconciliation and wholeness. Its enduring power lies in making peace itself a divine and human aspiration.

Vayechulu is the Torah’s account of the completion of creation, **Genesis 2:1–3**. Heaven and earth are finished; on the seventh day God ceases from the work of creation, blesses the day, and makes it holy. The passage establishes the theological foundation of **Shabbat**: sacred rest is rooted in creation itself. Human observance of the seventh day therefore echoes God’s own cessation and recognizes the created world as complete and purposeful.

The Friday-night abbreviated repetition of the Amidah centers on **God as Creator and sanctifier of Shabbat**. Rather than repeating the entire standing prayer, it condenses its themes into a blessing recalling creation, sacred rest, and the unique relationship between God, Shabbat, and Israel. The text emphasizes that the seventh day is both testimony to creation and a gift of holiness, joining cosmic order with the lived experience of sacred time.

Kaddish Titkabbal is an **Aramaic** form of Kaddish that adds a petition that the prayers and supplications of Israel be accepted before God. Like other forms of Kaddish, it magnifies God’s name, anticipates divine sovereignty, and asks for abundant peace. Its distinctive line—“May the prayers and supplications of all Israel be accepted”—connects communal prayer with hope that human words are heard and received with mercy.

Psalm 23, attributed to **King David**, portrays God as a shepherd who guides, nourishes, protects, and restores. Even through “the valley of the shadow of death,” the speaker fears no evil because God is present. The psalm moves from pastoral imagery to a banquet of abundance and concludes with confidence in lifelong divine goodness and mercy: “I shall dwell in the house of the Lord.” Biblical citation: **Psalm 23:1–6**.

Kaddish Shalem is an **Aramaic** doxology that magnifies God’s name, prays for divine sovereignty, and asks for abundant peace. Its distinctive petition asks that the prayers and supplications of Israel be accepted before God. The prayer contains no reference to death; even when connected with memorial moments, its language remains focused on God, communal prayer, and peace. The central response—“May His great name be blessed forever and ever”—is a public affirmation of faith.

Hashkabah is a **Sephardic memorial prayer** asking that the soul of the deceased be granted rest, peace, and a place among the righteous. Its name comes from the Hebrew root meaning “to lie down” or “rest,” reflecting the prayer’s image of death as repose under divine care. The text joins remembrance of a particular person with confidence in God’s mercy and the enduring bond between the living community and those it remembers.

Rogativo is a **Sephardic prayer for healing and mercy**, its name reflecting the Judeo-Spanish and Iberian sense of a supplication or earnest plea. The prayer asks God to remember the sick with compassion and grant healing, strength, and restoration. Its language places human vulnerability within a communal act of care: illness belongs to the individual, but the plea for healing belongs to the community. The prayer expresses hope without treating recovery as something human beings can command.

Parashah and announcements provide the service’s transition from fixed liturgy to the community’s current week. The parashah identifies the **Torah portion** that frames the congregation’s study and reflection, while announcements connect worship with upcoming programs, responsibilities, celebrations, and needs. This section helps carry the spirit of Shabbat from prayer into shared **communal life**.

Aleinu is especially at home on Rosh Hashanah because its proclamation of divine kingship belongs to the theological vocabulary of the day. The prayer is ancient, and its first paragraph also appears prominently in the Rosh Hashanah Musaf Malchuyot section; only later did Aleinu become a standard conclusion to daily services. Hearing it at the close of the evening service therefore carries an echo of its High Holiday setting: Israel bows before the sovereign of all, then looks toward a world in which that sovereignty is universally recognized.

Yigdal is a medieval metrical hymn traditionally attributed to Daniel ben Judah Dayyan, active in 14th-century Rome. Its achievement is unusually practical: it turns Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith into thirteen memorable poetic statements that can be sung and taught. De Sola Pool explicitly numbers the thirteen units and places the hymn near the close of Friday-evening worship, while also using it in the High Holiday books. The attribution is traditional rather than fully documentary, but the structure clearly follows Maimonides from divine unity through prophecy, Torah, reward and punishment, Messiah, and resurrection.

Shalom Aleichem is an anonymous early-modern hymn shaped by post-Safed Kabbalistic Sabbath practice. Its conceptual source is much older: Talmud Shabbat 119b describes two angels accompanying a person home on Friday night. De Sola Pool preserves its original domestic setting by placing it under the rubric for entering the home, not inside the synagogue service proper. The sequence is almost ceremonial: welcome the angels, ask their blessing, then send them in peace. That final dismissal has long puzzled readers, and the hymn's spread across Ashkenazi, Sephardic, Mizrahi, and Hasidic communities produced dramatically different melodies.

The traditional Sabbath blessings draw on the **Priestly Blessing, Numbers 6:24–26**: “May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make His face shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the Lord turn His face toward you and grant you peace.” The threefold blessing moves from protection to grace and finally to **shalom**, presenting peace as the culmination of blessing and a condition of wholeness.

Kiddush sanctifies Shabbat over wine by joining the **creation story** with the blessing over the fruit of the vine. Its central biblical passage recalls God’s completion of creation and sanctification of the seventh day (**Genesis 2:1–3**). The blessing then declares Shabbat holy, a remembrance of creation and of the Exodus. Kiddush presents sacred time as both cosmic and historical: creation, freedom, covenant, and holiness meet in the seventh day.

The Rosh Hashanah candle-lighting supplement explicitly provides wording for **Shabbat and festival lights** when the holiday begins Friday evening, followed by Shehecheyanu in Ladino, Hebrew, transliteration, and English. That makes candle lighting the service’s first double threshold: Shabbat and the new year enter together before synagogue prayer begins. Shehecheyanu then adds a second idea—gratitude not merely for the holiday, but for having lived to reach this particular moment.

Achot Ketanah was written by Abraham Hazan Gerondi, a 13th-century poet associated with Girona in Catalonia. De Sola Pool identifies it as a hymn for the first night of Rosh Hashanah, and its structure makes the placement unmistakable: stanza after stanza dismisses the old year until the final stanza reverses the refrain and welcomes the new year with blessing. The poem therefore does more than describe transition; it performs it. The little sister is Israel, and the repeated refrain turns communal lament into liturgical threshold drama.

The High Holiday Kaddish retains Kaddish’s Aramaic core: magnifying God’s name and praying for divine sovereignty and peace. Here it closes the Achot Ketanah unit and turns the congregation toward Barchu. Traditionally chanted to Achot Ketanah’s melody, it carries the piyyut’s musical atmosphere directly into the formal evening service.

Ki Hem Chayanu—“for they are our life”—comes from the blessing of divine love before the Shema and describes Torah not as information but as the substance of Jewish life. On Rosh Hashanah evening the line carries extra weight: the new year begins by locating life itself in covenant, learning, and the words Israel is about to recite in the Shema. The movement from God’s love to Torah to Shema makes this short Hebrew passage the hinge between being loved by God and answering that love with allegiance.

This passage is Numbers 10:10: on days of rejoicing, festivals, and new moons, Israel is commanded to sound trumpets over its offerings so that the day will be “for a memorial before your God.” On Rosh Hashanah the word memorial is especially striking. The verse links sacred time, sound, sacrifice, and remembrance long before the later rabbinic shofar liturgy developed. Read on the first evening of the year, it quietly anticipates one of the holiday’s central ideas: being remembered before God.

Kaddish L’Ela is a festival form of the familiar Aramaic doxology, magnifying God’s name and praying for divine sovereignty and peace. In this Rosh Hashanah evening sequence it comes immediately before the Amidah, so its function is to close the Shema-and-redemption unit and clear the way for the standing prayer. That placement matters: after proclaiming God’s unity and recalling redemption, the congregation now shifts from public declaration to direct encounter with God in the Amidah.

Ya'aleh V'Yavo is the festival insertion that asks God to remember Israel, the ancestors, Jerusalem, and the day itself for life, goodness, blessing, and peace. Its repeated verb—remember—belongs naturally to Rosh Hashanah, Yom HaZikaron, the Day of Remembrance. In the evening Amidah it quietly reinforces one of the holiday’s central themes: standing before God is also asking to be remembered favorably. The prayer therefore links the fixed festival formula with Rosh Hashanah’s larger language of memory and judgment.

Modim places thanksgiving near the end of an Amidah dominated on Rosh Hashanah by judgment, remembrance, and hope for life. Before leaving the prayer, the congregation names daily life and continuing mercy as gifts already received. The year therefore begins with gratitude beside uncertainty: not only asking what will be, but acknowledging what has already been given.

The Friday-night abbreviated repetition, often associated with Magen Avot, is a distinctive exception to the normal rule that the evening Amidah is not repeated. Rabbinic tradition established this shortened communal form for Friday night rather than a full repetition. On Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat, its presence is a reminder that the weekly Shabbat liturgy still shapes the festival service: creation, sacred rest, and God as Creator remain audible inside the New Year’s themes of judgment and kingship.

The second paragraph of Aleinu shifts from Israel’s present act of worship to a universal future: idolatry disappears, humanity recognizes one God, and divine sovereignty becomes visible throughout the world. On Rosh Hashanah this is especially pointed because kingship is one of the day’s governing themes. The paragraph ends with Zechariah 14:9—“the Lord shall be One and His name One”—so the service’s language of divine judgment ultimately opens outward into a vision of universal recognition rather than remaining only about Israel.

VeNeemar introduces Aleinu’s closing biblical proof-text, Zechariah 14:9: “The Lord shall be King over all the earth; on that day the Lord shall be One and His name One.” On Rosh Hashanah, the verse is more than a familiar conclusion. The day repeatedly names God as King, and this citation pushes that claim toward the future: divine sovereignty is not only confessed by the congregation now but imagined as something that will one day be recognized throughout the world.

The Rosh Hashanah blessings at the close of this service move the festival from synagogue liturgy back toward home and family. Their placement is significant: after the formal conclusion of prayer, the New Year is marked not only by themes of judgment and kingship but by spoken wishes for blessing, life, peace, and a good year. In the Leader Companion this is best understood as a practical ritual bridge—the congregation leaves the structured service and enters the lived observance of Rosh Hashanah.

Adonai Hu HaElohim opens the service with the biblical declaration “The Lord, He is God,” echoing the people’s response to Elijah on Mount Carmel in 1 Kings 18:39. On Rosh Hashanah morning it functions as an immediate statement of allegiance before the long liturgy begins. The repetition is simple but forceful: before speaking of judgment, remembrance, or merit, the congregation first establishes the most basic claim of the day—God alone is sovereign.

Nishmat Kol Chai—“The soul of every living being”—is an expansive hymn of **gratitude and praise**. It imagines that even if our mouths were filled with song like the sea and our tongues with melody like its waves, we could not adequately thank God for life, deliverance, and sustaining mercy. The prayer moves from the voice of all creation to Israel’s particular gratitude, emphasizing that divine goodness exceeds the human capacity to express thanks.

This English section translates Nishmat’s great thought experiment: even if the sea were song, the waves melody, the heavens parchment, and every limb devoted to praise, human beings still could not thank God adequately. Its importance is not merely poetic excess. The passage makes gratitude itself an exercise in humility: the more one tries to enumerate divine gifts—life, rescue, sight, movement, speech—the clearer it becomes that thanksgiving can never fully catch up with what has been received.

B’Fi Yesharim is the closing crescendo of Nishmat. It imagines praise coming from successive groups—the upright, righteous, faithful, and holy—before Israel joins them in blessing God. The liturgical movement is from universal gratitude toward a structured chorus of human voices. In the morning service, this passage is the bridge from Nishmat’s expansive poetry into the formal blessing of Yishtabach, concentrating an enormous meditation on praise into a communal declaration.

This English reading renders the sequence behind B’Fi Yesharim: praise rises through the upright, righteous, faithful, holy, and finally through Israel. The progression is more than a list of flattering titles. It imagines worship as cumulative, each community adding another voice until praise becomes collective. In the Rosh Hashanah morning service, that widening chorus is a useful counterpoint to the individual anxiety of judgment: the worshipper stands not alone, but inside a people whose praise spans generations and spiritual types.

Yede Rashim is a **first-day Rosh Hashanah hymn by Judah Halevi** (c. 1075–1141), the great Hebrew poet of medieval Spain. De Sola Pool pairs it with Halevi’s Yehe Shmech on the second day, creating a deliberate two-day Spanish-Portuguese program. The poem makes spiritual poverty the basis of prayer: Israel approaches without boasting of its own strength, yet still joins the language of holiness. The pairing is more interesting than either poem alone—two days, one poet, two different approaches to praise.

Yehe Shmech is a **second-day Rosh Hashanah hymn by Judah Halevi** (c. 1075–1141), the major poet of medieval al-Andalus. De Sola Pool places it opposite Halevi’s Yede Rashim on day one, making the two poems a curated pair rather than unrelated insertions. Yehe Shmech expands human praise into celestial and angelic praise, fitting Rosh Hashanah’s imagery of the heavenly court. The exact date and place of this individual poem are unknown, but its medieval Spanish authorship is secure.

This passage is recited **only when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat**. Its presence signals that the festival has not replaced the weekly Sabbath; Shabbat reshapes the morning liturgy even on the Day of Judgment. The text praises the special rest and holiness of the seventh day, creating an important contrast: Rosh Hashanah asks us to confront time, mortality, and accountability, while Shabbat insists that sacred life also requires stopping, delight, and trust.

summaries.summary: This passage belongs to the blessing that praises God as Creator of light and the heavenly order. Its language moves from the physical cosmos to the angelic court, where celestial beings respond in awe and holiness. On Rosh Hashanah morning, that movement matters: the service repeatedly imagines God as King and Judge, but here human prayer joins a larger universe already oriented toward divine sovereignty. The worshipper is not creating holiness; the worshipper is entering a chorus imagined as already underway.

“Holy, holy, holy” comes from Isaiah 6:3, where seraphim proclaim God’s holiness in the prophet’s throne-room vision. The triple declaration is one of the Bible’s most powerful images of heavenly worship. In this morning blessing it is recited rather than functioning as the congregational Kedushah of the Amidah, but the imagery is the same: earthly prayer borrows the language of angels. On Rosh Hashanah, the throne-room setting naturally reinforces the day’s imagery of divine kingship and judgment.

This English passage continues the morning blessing’s vision of the heavenly hosts. Angels do not praise independently; they answer one another, creating a model of responsive worship. That image helps explain why so much Jewish liturgy is antiphonal: leader and congregation imitate a celestial pattern of call and response. On Rosh Hashanah, when worship can feel intensely personal, the passage insists that holiness is voiced communally—one voice prompts another, and praise becomes something no individual can complete alone.

This passage asks God to hasten redemption and gather Israel, moving the morning blessing from cosmic praise toward historical hope. The shift is significant: the God who orders sun, stars, and angels is also asked to act within human history. On Rosh Hashanah, that combination keeps divine kingship from becoming abstract. The sovereignty celebrated in heaven is expected to have consequences on earth—restoration, gathering, and renewed relationship between God and Israel.

Bocher b’amo Yisrael b’ahavah—“who chooses His people Israel in love”—is the closing line of Ahavah Rabbah, the morning blessing immediately before the Shema. The blessing moves from God’s love for Israel to Torah, learning, and covenant, then ends by naming divine choice as an act of love. Its placement matters: before Israel declares God’s unity in the Shema, the liturgy first frames the relationship as reciprocal—God loves and chooses Israel, and Israel responds with love, study, and allegiance.

summaries.prayerAction: True It Is -> Blessed Be He
summaries.summary: This blessing following the Shema emphasizes that God’s word is **true, enduring, and trustworthy** across generations. In the morning liturgy, truth is immediately tied to the Exodus: Israel’s faith rests not only on abstract belief but on remembered redemption. On Rosh Hashanah, that historical memory offers a counterweight to uncertainty about the coming year. The future is unknown, but the prayer grounds confidence in a covenantal past that the community continues to retell and affirm.

Mi Chamocha quotes the Song at the Sea, Exodus 15:11, asking who among all powers can compare with God. In the Rosh Hashanah morning service it places divine kingship inside the story of liberation: Israel first recognizes God’s incomparable sovereignty not in a palace but at the moment of escape from slavery. That matters for the holiday’s theology. The King before whom humanity is judged is also the Redeemer who acts in history, defeats oppression, and makes freedom possible.

Gaal Yisrael concludes the blessing of redemption immediately before the Amidah. It recalls the Exodus not as a closed historical event but as evidence of God’s continuing identity as Israel’s Redeemer. The placement is deliberate: Jewish prayer traditionally moves from redemption directly into standing before God. On Rosh Hashanah morning, that sequence tempers the anxiety of judgment. The congregation approaches the Judge only after remembering that this same God has already acted to save, liberate, and keep covenant.

The Rosh Hashanah Shacharit Amidah keeps the familiar architecture of the standing prayer but inserts the New Year’s language of **life, remembrance, kingship, and judgment**. Because the day may also be Shabbat, some forms include additional Sabbath wording, making the prayer sensitive to the calendar actually being observed. This Amidah is therefore not interchangeable with the evening version or Musaf: it belongs specifically to the morning service and prepares the congregation for Torah reading, shofar, and the much larger Musaf theology that follows.

Kedushah is a proclamation of **God’s holiness** built around biblical visions of heavenly worship. Its central declaration, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory,” comes from **Isaiah 6:3**. It also incorporates Ezekiel 3:12, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from His place.” Kedushah imagines earthly worship joining the angels in acknowledging a God whose holiness transcends creation yet fills the world.

summaries.prayerAction: We Thank Thee -> Our Hope on Thee
summaries.summary: Modim, the thanksgiving blessing of the Amidah, is strategically important on Rosh Hashanah morning. A service dominated by judgment and requests for life could easily become entirely petitionary; Modim interrupts that instinct. Before asking what the new year will bring, the worshipper acknowledges life, daily miracles, protection, and mercy already received. Gratitude therefore becomes part of judgment’s spiritual discipline: the year is not approached only as a problem to be solved, but as a gift already partly in hand.

Hayom—“Today”—is a compact High Holiday response built around the urgency of the present moment. Its petitions ask that **today** God strengthen, bless, exalt, and favor the congregation, ending with the hope of inscription for life. The repeated word is the point: Rosh Hashanah theology can sound cosmic and abstract, but Hayom pulls everything back into the immediate day. Judgment, mercy, and renewal are not postponed concepts; they are liturgical claims about what is happening now.

This English passage extends the Amidah’s closing hopes beyond survival toward the quality of life being requested: peace, blessing, dignity, and a life shaped by divine favor. On Rosh Hashanah, that distinction matters. The liturgy does not merely ask to be written into a book of biological existence; it imagines what a worthy year would contain. The request therefore turns “life” from a number of days into a moral and communal vision of how those days might actually be lived.

Avinu Malkeinu combines two names for God—**Father and King**—and uses that tension to hold intimacy and judgment together. Taanit 25b connects its core formula with Rabbi Akiva during a drought. In this service it is specifically **omitted on Shabbat**, an important calendar distinction: when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, the weekday-style supplicatory litany gives way to the Sabbath’s different liturgical character. Its absence can therefore be as meaningful as its recitation.

“May you be answered” is a congregational bridge from the completed Shacharit into the next stage of the service. Its language asks that prayer be accepted and that divine response come with mercy. On Rosh Hashanah morning the placement is significant: the community has just finished an intense Amidah and is about to move toward special piyyutim, communal petitions, and Torah service. The text functions almost like a liturgical acknowledgment that prayer has been offered, but its outcome is still being entrusted to God.

Lema’ancha Elohai is a **first-day Rosh Hashanah hymn attributed by de Sola Pool to David ben Saadia**; his exact identity, date, and place remain uncertain. The poem’s argument is striking: it does not claim that Israel deserves mercy, but repeatedly pleads “for Your own sake, O God.” God’s own name, covenant, and reputation for compassion become the basis of the appeal. Its responsorial form keeps returning the congregation to the urgent request that God hear, act, and not delay.

Ya’ane B’Boker Avot is a **second-day Rosh Hashanah hymn by Abraham ibn Ezra** (1089–1164/67), the Spanish-born poet, commentator, grammarian, and famously itinerant scholar. It answers the first day’s Lema’ancha Elohai with a different argument for mercy: **zechut avot**, the merit of the ancestors. Abraham’s trials and the patriarchal covenant become evidence in Israel’s plea. De Sola Pool’s refrain invokes God’s faithfulness to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, turning biblical ancestry into liturgical advocacy.

The Prayer for the Government reflects an old Jewish principle: communities pray for the welfare of the civil authorities under whom they live. Jeremiah 29:7 urges exiles to seek the peace of the city, and Pirkei Avot 3:2 warns of the danger of social disorder. In a Spanish-Portuguese service this prayer also reflects a long diaspora tradition of publicly expressing loyalty and civic responsibility. On Rosh Hashanah, communal judgment is therefore connected with the wellbeing of the broader society.

The Prayer for the Congregation turns the service’s focus inward from the state and public authorities to the local Jewish community. It asks blessing for those who sustain communal life, support worship, perform acts of charity, and care for the congregation’s institutions and members. On Rosh Hashanah this is especially apt: judgment is often imagined individually, but Jewish religious life is maintained collectively. The prayer reminds the leader that a congregation survives because ordinary people repeatedly choose to carry it.

summaries.prayerAction: Prayer for the State of Israel
summaries.summary: The Prayer for the State of Israel asks divine protection and guidance for **Medinat Yisrael**, its leaders, defenders, and people. Composed after the establishment of the State in 1948, the prayer is commonly associated with Israel’s Chief Rabbinate and Rabbi Yitzhak HaLevi Herzog. It frames Jewish sovereignty in covenantal language, asking that the state be strengthened, its inhabitants protected, and the Jewish people gathered in peace and security.

Synagogue honors—such as aliyot, opening the Hekhal, or carrying the Torah—formally allocated by the synagogue’s congregational officers. In many Jewish communities these honors were publicly bid for because they were limited, desirable privileges; bidding provided an orderly way to decide who would receive them while also raising money for synagogue and charitable needs. The custom was widespread across many Jewish communities and became especially visible in many Sephardic settings. In S&P practice, bidding joins ritual honor, communal giving, and orderly allocation of scarce privileges.

This reading appears **only when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat**. It brings explicit Sabbath language into the transition toward Torah service, reminding the congregation that the day is governed by two sacred calendars at once. The text praises God’s works and the gift of holy rest. Its conditional presence is itself worth noticing: Rosh Hashanah does not suspend Shabbat; rather, the festival must be experienced through the additional holiness and restrictions of the seventh day.

This passage prepares the congregation for Torah service by shifting from praise toward direct recognition of God’s uniqueness and authority. Its role is transitional: after the personal and communal prayers of Shacharit, attention turns toward revelation and the public reading of Torah. On Rosh Hashanah that movement is important because the day’s theology is not built from prayer alone. The congregation will soon hear biblical narratives chosen specifically to frame the meanings of memory, birth, covenant, sacrifice, and mercy.

Vayehi Binso’a quotes **Numbers 10:35–36**, the words Moses proclaimed when the Ark set out and when it came to rest. The verses ask God to arise, scatter enemies, and return to the “myriads of Israel.” The passage connects the Torah scroll with the biblical Ark and Israel’s wilderness journey. Its imagery presents Torah not as a static object but as a source of divine presence accompanying the people on their journey.

Kohanecha draws on Psalm 132:9: “Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and Your faithful sing for joy.” In the Torah service it imagines the sanctuary community properly ordered around holiness—priests, righteous service, and rejoicing. The verse comes from a psalm concerned with David, Zion, and God’s dwelling place, so its use while the Ark is open gives ancient Temple imagery a new liturgical setting. The Torah scroll becomes the focal point around which sacred service is organized.

Adonai Adonai proclaims the **Thirteen Attributes of Mercy** from **Exodus 34:6–7**, revealed after the sin of the Golden Calf. God is described as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness and truth, preserving mercy, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. The passage became one of Judaism’s central texts of repentance because it grounds the possibility of forgiveness in God’s own character: justice remains real, but mercy makes return possible.

summaries.prayerAction: In the Spirit -> Life of Blessing
summaries.summary: This English meditation follows the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and asks that the spirit of divine compassion shape the coming year. The sequence matters: Exodus 34 does not remain a historical quotation; the service turns God’s attributes into a present plea for a life of blessing. On Rosh Hashanah, when judgment is central, the prayer insists that judgment is addressed to a God already described as compassionate, gracious, patient, and abundant in mercy.

This reading asks that the merit and virtue of earlier generations help perfect the community now. It reflects the classical Jewish idea of **zechut avot**, ancestral merit: the covenantal lives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the righteous are invoked not as substitutes for present responsibility but as grounds for mercy. On Rosh Hashanah, that argument appears repeatedly. The congregation asks to be judged as itself, yet also as the latest generation in a relationship extending far beyond its own accomplishments.

This “May the words” passage is a **Yehi Ratzon**, a personal petition that asks God to accept both spoken prayer and inward intention. The distinction matters in a long High Holiday service: liturgical correctness is not enough if attention and purpose are absent. The prayer therefore functions as a self-check before the Torah procession continues. Rosh Hashanah repeatedly asks what is being judged; this small text answers that both public words and private interior life belong within the scope of worship.

summaries.prayerAction: Blessed Be Thy Name -> Is Thine
summaries.summary: “Blessed be Your Name” is a brief act of praise during the open-Ark sequence. Its importance is less in doctrinal novelty than in placement: the congregation is physically oriented toward the Torah scrolls while verbally insisting that ultimate holiness belongs to God, not to the objects themselves. The scrolls are honored because they bear divine teaching. This distinction is especially useful in a ceremonial moment when visual ritual is strong—the honor shown to Torah is a form of honoring the God whose word it contains.

Bei Ana is an Aramaic supplication associated with the Torah service, expressing trust in God and asking for goodness, life, and peace. Its language belongs to the distinctive Sephardic ceremonial world surrounding the Torah procession. The use of Aramaic is itself notable: just as Kaddish preserves a communal Jewish language older than many modern vernaculars, Bei Ana gives the Torah service a historical texture different from the surrounding Hebrew and English. Its petitions keep ceremony tied to concrete hopes for life and wellbeing.

Gadlu combines biblical verses inviting the community to **magnify God together**. Its central line, “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt His name together,” comes from Psalm 34:4, attributed to King David. The response, “Yours, O Lord, are greatness, power, glory, victory, and majesty,” draws from 1 Chronicles 29:11. Together the verses frame communal worship as shared recognition of divine greatness rather than an individual act.

A Torah procession carries the scrolls visibly through the worshipping community, turning movement into part of the service rather than mere logistics. Whether the scrolls are being taken out or returned, the procession honors Torah as a living communal inheritance and gives the congregation a physical relationship to the text it is about to hear or has just heard. The accompanying verses and songs vary by service, but the basic action is the same: Torah moves from the Ark into the midst of the congregation and back again.

Rommemu, Torah Tziva, and Etz Chaim form a compact theology of Torah through several biblical images. The congregation first exalts God, then identifies Torah as the inheritance commanded through Moses, and finally calls it a **tree of life** to those who hold fast to it. The sequence moves from God to revelation to lived attachment. During Rosh Hashanah’s Torah service, that movement matters: renewal is not imagined only as emotion or judgment, but as recommitment to a received way of life.

This cue assigns the person who will perform Hagbah, raising the Torah scroll so the congregation can see the written text. The action follows the Torah reading and turns the scroll itself into the focus of communal attention before Vezot HaTorah. In the Leader's Companion this is primarily an operational cue: make the honor clear before the scroll is lifted so the service can proceed without hesitation.

V’Zot HaTorah—“This is the Torah”—quotes **Deuteronomy 4:44**: “This is the Torah that Moses set before the children of Israel.” The declaration identifies the Torah scroll being held before the congregation with the Torah transmitted through Moses. Its brevity gives the physical scroll symbolic force: the text before the community represents the continuing covenant, teaching, and inheritance of Israel, linking the present congregation to Sinai and the generations that preserved Torah.

The Torah blessings frame public reading as an act of covenant rather than information. The blessing before the reading praises God for choosing Israel and giving Torah; the blessing after thanks God for giving a Torah of truth and planting eternal life within the people. Each aliyah therefore reenacts the relationship between revelation and community. On Rosh Hashanah, the blessings are the fixed frame around readings that differ by day, making the changing narratives part of one continuous covenantal act.

summaries.prayerAction: Sermons for First and Second Day

summaries.summary: Et Sha’arei Ratzon was written by **Judah ben Samuel ibn Abbas**, a 12th-century Sephardic poet associated with Fez and later Aleppo. It became one of the signature Sephardic Rosh Hashanah Akedah poems. De Sola Pool places it immediately before the shofar material, making the ram of Genesis 22 a direct bridge to the horn about to be sounded. The poem dramatically expands the biblical story with dialogue and midrashic material, including Sarah’s anguish, turning ancestral memory into an urgent plea for mercy.

These individual paragraphs are the dramatic interior of **Et Sha’arei Ratzon**, the Sephardic Akedah piyyut. The poem expands Genesis 22 with dialogue, emotion, and later tradition, allowing Abraham, Isaac, and even Sarah’s anguish to enter the service. Their purpose is not simply to retell the binding of Isaac but to make the ancestral ordeal emotionally present before the shofar. The ram that replaces Isaac links the poem naturally to the instrument about to be sounded.

The shofar service turns the Torah’s brief command for a day of sounding into one of Rosh Hashanah’s defining rituals. The blasts are not words, yet the liturgy surrounds them with themes of kingship, remembrance, Sinai, repentance, and future redemption. **When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, the shofar is not sounded in the synagogue**, following rabbinic law. That absence dramatically changes the morning service: the day remains Rosh Hashanah, but its most recognizable sound is deliberately withheld.

Adonai B’Kol Shofar is headed by de Sola Pool as a hymn by “Jacob” for the weekday shofar ceremony; the exact poet is historically unresolved. Its placement immediately before shofar gives the poem its force: the horn becomes not only the Rosh Hashanah instrument but the future signal of ingathering and redemption. The poem asks for exiles to return and Zion to be restored. **It is not used when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat**, because the shofar ceremony itself is omitted.

Standing is a recurring liturgical posture marking moments of heightened communal attention: the opening of the Ark, the Torah procession, Barchu, the Amidah, memorial prayer, or another solemn transition. The cue is operational rather than a separate prayer, but it is important because posture helps the congregation recognize that the service has entered a new ritual state. In the Leader's Companion, this summary should be read generically; the specific reason for standing is supplied by the surrounding service cues.

The shofar blessings identify the act before any sound is made: one blessing commands hearing the shofar, and Shehecheyanu thanks God for reaching this occasion. The caller then announces the sequence of **tekiah, shevarim, and teruah** so blower and congregation know what is required. These calls are recited only when shofar is actually sounded; on Shabbat Rosh Hashanah they disappear with the blasts. The ritual therefore combines precise legal form with one of the service’s most emotional moments.

Shofar blowing uses several distinct sounds: tekiah, a sustained note; shevarim, broken sigh-like notes; and teruah, rapid staccato blasts. Rabbinic tradition preserves uncertainty about the exact biblical teruah, so the service combines patterns to satisfy the possibilities. On Rosh Hashanah that legal precision produces an intentionally wordless moment. When the festival falls on Shabbat, however, the synagogue does not blow shofar; the silence is a deliberate rabbinic observance, not an omission or production error.

Ashrei centers on Psalm 145, an alphabetic acrostic praising God’s kingship and care for creation. One famous feature is the **missing nun verse** in the Masoretic text; the alphabet jumps from mem to samekh. Berakhot 4b links daily recitation of Ashrei with its alphabetical structure and the verse “You open Your hand,” which portrays God sustaining all life. Here, after shofar and Torah service, Ashrei begins the transition back toward the Ark and then Musaf.

Yimloch—“The Lord will reign forever”—draws on biblical kingship language as the Torah is returned. On Rosh Hashanah this familiar procession verse sounds unusually central because **Malchuyot**, divine kingship, will soon become one of Musaf’s three great themes. The procession therefore anticipates Musaf before it formally begins. The Torah returns to the Ark while the congregation declares that God’s reign extends beyond the immediate ceremony and beyond any single generation.

Psalm 29, Mizmor L’David, attributed to **King David**, portrays the **voice of God** as a force moving through creation. The divine voice thunders over waters, breaks cedars, flashes fire, and shakes the wilderness, while all in God’s temple proclaim glory. The psalm concludes by moving from overwhelming power to blessing: the God who reigns over the flood gives strength to the people and blesses them with peace. Biblical citation: Psalm 29:1–11.

Shuvah draws on biblical verses asking God to **return and restore**. The language echoes **Numbers 10:36**, Moses’ words when the Ark came to rest: “Return, O Lord, to the myriads of Israel,” and other verses expressing longing for divine presence and renewal. Its central idea is reciprocal return: Israel seeks God while asking God to return to Israel. The prayer turns restoration into both a spiritual and communal hope.

summaries.prayerAction: I Wait on the Lord -> Gives It Voice
summaries.summary: “I wait on the Lord” introduces Musaf with the language of expectation. After the Torah service and, on a weekday Rosh Hashanah, the shofar blasts, the congregation enters the day’s most elaborate Amidah. Waiting is therefore an apt spiritual posture: the service has already spoken, read, remembered, and sounded, yet the central theological work is still ahead. The passage gives voice to patience and attentiveness before Musaf turns to kingship, remembrance, and shofarot in extended biblical form.

The Musaf Amidah is the theological center of Rosh Hashanah morning. Unlike Shacharit, it contains the great triptych of **Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot**—Kingship, Remembrance, and Shofar—each developed through biblical verses and concluding blessing. Musaf also recalls the additional Temple offering of the day. When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, the wording reflects both sanctities, while the shofar-blowing moments normally embedded in the service are omitted. The prayer therefore changes with the calendar without losing its central structure.

**Malchuyot—Kingship** is the first of Rosh Hashanah Musaf’s three signature sections. It gathers biblical verses proclaiming God as King and asks the congregation to accept divine sovereignty. This is also the original liturgical home of Aleinu, long before Aleinu became a standard conclusion to daily services. On a non-Shabbat Rosh Hashanah the section is followed by shofar blasts; on Shabbat those blasts are omitted, but the theology of kingship remains fully intact.

Aleinu appears here in its **older Rosh Hashanah setting**, inside Malchuyot, rather than merely as a familiar closing prayer. Its first paragraph contrasts Israel’s worship of the one God with idolatry; its second imagines a future when all humanity recognizes divine sovereignty. That makes Aleinu almost a miniature Malchuyot: present allegiance opens toward universal kingship. Hearing it here restores a context often hidden by its everyday use at the end of services.

This English passage belongs to Malchuyot and asks God to establish Israel’s portion in holiness while sanctifying the **Day of Remembrance**. Its placement shows how kingship is not treated as political metaphor alone. Accepting God as King is tied to how the day itself is ordered—its holiness, its covenantal identity, and the community’s place within it. The prayer moves from universal sovereignty back to the concrete request that this particular congregation be granted a meaningful share in the sacred day.

U’Dvarcha closes the Malchuyot movement by affirming that God’s word is enduring and that the day is **Yom HaZikaron, the Day of Remembrance**. The line links kingship with memory: the divine King is not distant but remembers covenant, history, and human lives. In Musaf, this also prepares the transition toward Zichronot, where remembrance becomes the explicit subject. The service’s three major themes are therefore not isolated chapters; each one begins to open into the next.

These Musaf shofar calls announce the blasts that follow Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot. Unlike the earlier pre-blowing sequence, they do not introduce a new blessing; they punctuate the three theological sections and turn ideas into sound. The same categories—tekiah, shevarim, and teruah—recur, but their meaning changes with context: kingship, memory, and revelation/redemption have just been proclaimed. **On Shabbat these calls and blasts are omitted**, while the surrounding Musaf texts remain.

Hayom Harat Olam—“Today is the birthday of the world”—is recited after each of the three central Musaf sections when the shofar is sounded. It imagines all creation standing in judgment and asks whether God will treat humanity as children or servants. The repeated text changes meaning by context: after Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot, the same words absorb the theme just completed. **On Shabbat, these shofar-linked repetitions are omitted with the blasts**, preserving the Sabbath form of the service.

**Zichronot—Remembrances** is the second great section of the Rosh Hashanah Musaf Amidah. Its biblical verses trace divine remembrance from Noah and the covenant through Israel’s history, insisting that nothing is forgotten before God. Rosh Hashanah is therefore not only a day when individuals try to remember their own deeds; it is a day when the congregation asks to be held within God’s faithful memory. On non-Shabbat years, shofar blasts follow the section; on Shabbat the remembrance remains while the blasts are omitted.

summaries.prayerAction: Our God -> Divine King Art Thou
summaries.summary: This passage opens the heart of Zichronot by addressing God as the One who remembers what human beings cannot. The prayer’s memory is not simple recollection: in biblical Hebrew, divine “remembering” often means turning memory into action, as when God remembers Noah or the covenant. That gives the section its urgency. The congregation is not asking merely to be noticed; it is asking that covenantal memory become mercy, life, and favorable judgment in the year ahead.

V’Ain Shikhecha—“there is no forgetting before You”—states the central theology of Zichronot with almost frightening clarity. Human memory is selective and fragile; divine memory is imagined as complete. Yet the passage immediately balances that idea with **zokher habrit**, God as One who remembers the covenant. The same perfect memory that makes judgment serious also makes mercy possible, because God remembers promises, ancestors, and relationship alongside failure. Rosh Hashanah remembrance is therefore covenantal, not merely forensic.

**Shofarot** is the third and final signature section of Rosh Hashanah Musaf. Its biblical verses move through different meanings of the shofar: revelation at Sinai, divine majesty, worship, and the future horn of redemption. The instrument therefore carries past, present, and future at once. On a weekday Rosh Hashanah, actual shofar blasts punctuate the conclusion; **on Shabbat, the verses remain but the instrument is silent**. The liturgy preserves the idea of shofar even when Jewish law withholds the sound.

Psalm 150 is the final psalm in the Psalter and a catalogue of instruments used to praise God—trumpet or shofar, harp, lyre, drum, strings, flute, and cymbals. In **Shofarot**, its placement is especially pointed: the shofar is heard as one instrument inside a much larger biblical orchestra of praise. The psalm ends by widening beyond instruments altogether: “Let every breath praise the Lord.” Sound begins with ritual instruments and culminates in life itself becoming praise.

Ani Adonai Eloheichem anchors Shofarot in God’s self-identification: “I am the Lord your God.” The section’s many trumpet and shofar verses could otherwise become a catalogue of dramatic sound; this passage brings them back to covenant. The shofar matters because it belongs to a relationship between God and Israel—at Sinai, in worship, and in hopes for redemption. Near the close of Shofarot, the text turns acoustic imagery into a renewed statement of who is being addressed and why the sound matters.

Birkat Kohanim comes from Numbers 6:24–26, but archaeology gives these verses an extraordinary afterlife: versions of the blessing appear on the **Ketef Hinnom silver amulets** from the late First Temple period, among the oldest surviving biblical texts. In Musaf the blessing asks for protection, grace, and finally peace. On Rosh Hashanah, that final movement toward shalom is especially powerful: after kingship, remembrance, judgment, and shofar, the service still imagines divine blessing reaching its fullest expression in peace.

This peace blessing follows the extraordinary intensity of Musaf and asks that divine favor settle into **shalom**—not only the absence of conflict, but wholeness and stability. Its placement is the theological landing point of the Amidah. After the congregation has proclaimed kingship, appealed to divine memory, and heard or imagined the shofar, the service does not end in judgment. It ends by asking what all that sacred drama is for: a life capable of blessing, coherence, and peace.

“You who cleave to the Lord your God are all alive today” echoes Deuteronomy 4:4 and turns **life** into a covenantal category. On Rosh Hashanah, when inscription for life is repeated throughout the liturgy, the verse gives that hope a spiritual dimension: life is not only something granted from outside but something associated with attachment to God. The reading therefore links the holiday’s urgent petitions for life with the older Torah language of fidelity, relationship, and continued communal existence.

U’Vsefer Chayim asks that Israel be remembered and inscribed in the **Book of Life, blessing, peace, and good sustenance**. The phrase expands what “life” means: the prayer does not ask for mere continuation but for a life containing peace and blessing. Placed near the end of Musaf, it gathers the holiday’s recurring book imagery into a final petition. After long theological sections about kingship and memory, the request becomes direct and personal again: write us into a good year.

“May you be answered” at the Gates marks another liturgical threshold near the close of the service. Gate imagery is especially suited to the High Holidays because prayer repeatedly imagines access—doors of mercy, repentance, and acceptance that may open or close. Here the language asks that the congregation’s petitions pass through those gates favorably. The prayer is brief, but after the length of Musaf it gives the leader a useful interpretive frame: the central question is no longer what was said, but whether the prayer will be received.

Ein Keloheinu is an **anonymous medieval hymn**; no author, exact date, or place is securely known. Its literary interest is structural: successive blocks move through Ein (“there is none”), Mi (“who is like”), Nodeh (“let us thank”), Barukh (“blessed”), and Atah Hu (“You are”), while cycling through divine titles. De Sola Pool places it near the close of both Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur morning services, confirming established Spanish-Portuguese High Holiday use. Its theology works through patterned repetition rather than argument.

Mourner’s Kaddish is an **Aramaic** declaration of God’s greatness and holiness. Despite its association with mourning, it contains no reference to death; instead it magnifies God’s name and prays for divine sovereignty and abundant peace. The mourner’s act of praising God in the presence of loss gives the prayer much of its emotional force. Its repeated congregational response, “May His great name be blessed forever and ever,” transforms private grief into communal affirmation.

Adon Olam is an **anonymous medieval hymn**; its common attribution to Solomon ibn Gabirol is not secure. De Sola Pool places it at the conclusion of both Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur morning services. Its most striking move is scale: the poem begins with God reigning before creation and after existence ends, then suddenly becomes intimate as the worshipper entrusts body and spirit to God. That journey from cosmos to individual makes it especially effective at the end of a service dominated by divine kingship.

summaries.prayerAction: Candle Lighting for the Six Million
summaries.summary: This opening candle is dedicated to the **six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust**, placing communal memory at the threshold of Yom Kippur. Before the service turns to individual confession, the congregation first remembers lives destroyed by persecution and mass murder. The act changes the emotional scale of the evening: repentance begins not only with private moral accounting but with Jewish historical memory. A single flame becomes a deliberately inadequate symbol for millions of lives, communities, languages, families, and futures that were extinguished.

Yom Kippur candle lighting marks the last ordinary act before the fast fully takes hold. The blessing sanctifies the lights of the holy day, but their symbolism is unusually layered: illumination, soul, memory, and the fragile persistence of life. On Kol Nidrei night, when the congregation is about to confront mortality and judgment, the act of creating light is itself a quiet theological statement. The day begins not in darkness, but with a deliberate flame carried into the hours of fasting and confession.

Va’ani opens with the biblical posture of entering God’s house in reverence and mercy. On Kol Nidrei night that language is especially charged: the congregation is not simply arriving for another evening service but entering the most solemn liturgical night of the year. The prayer balances access with humility—one comes before God only through divine lovingkindness, not personal entitlement. As an opening reading, it sets the spiritual stance for everything that follows: presence, awe, dependence, and readiness to be judged.

Wearing a tallit at night is unusual, which is exactly why the Kol Nidrei blessing is worth noticing. The custom is to put on the tallit **before sunset**, while it is still day, so the mitzvah blessing can be recited. The white garment also becomes part of Yom Kippur’s visual language of purity and mortality. Before Kol Nidrei begins, the worshipper is physically wrapped in a commandment, turning repentance from an idea into something worn on the body.

Psalm 93, attributed to **King David**, proclaims God as king, clothed in majesty and strength. The stability of the world reflects divine sovereignty, while the roaring seas symbolize forces of chaos that God surpasses in power. The psalm moves from cosmic kingship to the holiness of God’s house, declaring that divine testimonies are trustworthy and holiness endures. Biblical citation: **Psalm 93:1–5**.

Before the Kol Nidrei Torah ceremony, de Sola Pool directs the Reader to announce those designated for the evening's ritual honors, including opening the Ark, carrying and accompanying the Torah scrolls, assisting the Reader, and other service roles. The announcement makes the distribution of honors public and orderly before the scrolls are removed. In this service the cue is best understood as an operational assignment of honors rather than as part of the prayer text itself.

This cue marks the transition into the Torah-centered ceremony that frames Kol Nidrei. Both de Sola Pool and Machzor Lev Shalem associate the opening of the Ark and removal of the Torah scrolls with the congregation standing. The posture is not incidental: the scrolls give the coming declaration a visible covenantal setting, and the congregation's rising signals that the service has moved from introductory preparation into a solemn public ritual centered on Torah.

summaries.prayerAction: Open Ark / Take Out / Adorn Torah Scrolls
summaries.summary: The Ark is opened and the Torah scrolls are removed and prepared for the Kol Nidrei ceremony. De Sola Pool places the scrolls at the center of the ritual sequence, while Machzor Lev Shalem likewise directs the congregation to rise as the Ark is opened and the scrolls are taken out. Their presence makes Kol Nidrei more than a private meditation: the declaration is made publicly, before the congregation, in the visible presence of Torah and communal authority.

B’Yeshiva Shel Ma’alah is the formal declaration that **permits prayer with transgressors**, a striking legal-liturgical preface to Kol Nidrei. It invokes both the heavenly and earthly courts and announces that the community will pray together with those who have sinned. The point is not to divide the room into righteous and guilty; on Yom Kippur the entire congregation stands in need of repentance. Before vows are addressed, the service first establishes who is allowed inside the circle of prayer: everyone.

Kol Nidrei is an Aramaic legal-liturgical declaration with Geonic roots. The Spanish-Portuguese rite uses retrospective wording, referring to vows since the previous Yom Kippur. It does not cancel juridical oaths, contracts, or obligations between people. Intoned three times by the rabbi “with profound solemnity,” this narrow legal formula became Yom Kippur’s emotional portal.

summaries.prayerAction: Kol Nidrei - Every Kind of Vow

summaries.summary: Shehecheyanu thanks God **“who has kept us alive, sustained us, and enabled us to reach this time.”** The blessing expresses gratitude not merely for an event but for the gift of being alive to experience it. Its three verbs move from life, to sustenance, to arrival, making the present moment itself an object of thanksgiving. The blessing turns awareness of time into spiritual consciousness: reaching a meaningful moment is never taken for granted.

After the Kol Nidrei ceremony, the Torah scrolls are carried back and replaced in the Ark. De Sola Pool directs that Psalm 29 be chanted during the return procession and that the Ark remain open while the following return prayers continue. On Yom Kippur the physical act of returning the scrolls also resonates with the day's central language of teshuvah—return—without changing the practical purpose of the cue: restore the scrolls reverently and complete the Torah ceremony before Maariv continues.

“Return, O Lord” accompanies the Torah scrolls back toward the Ark and echoes the biblical language surrounding the Ark’s journeys. On Kol Nidrei night, however, the word **return** carries an unavoidable second meaning: teshuvah itself is return. The physical motion of the Torahs back to their place therefore mirrors the spiritual motion demanded by the day. The ceremony turns movement into metaphor—the scrolls return to the Ark while the congregation begins the work of returning to covenant, community, and God.

This passage appeals to God’s mercy immediately after the Torahs are returned. Its placement is important: the grandeur of the Kol Nidrei ceremony gives way to direct dependence on compassion. Yom Kippur does not assume that solemnity itself earns forgiveness. The prayer instead asks the merciful God to continue sustaining a people who have failed. In the architecture of the evening, it is one of the moments where pageantry is deliberately stripped away and the service returns to the basic High Holiday claim that repentance requires divine mercy.

summaries.prayerAction: Blessed Art Thou -> Thy People Israel
summaries.summary: This blessing is part of the evening service’s praise of God as the One who orders darkness, light, and the heavens. On Kol Nidrei night that ordinary Maariv theme takes on unusual force: daylight has ended, the fast has begun, and the congregation is crossing into a sacred period governed by a different rhythm of time. The blessing reminds the worshipper that Yom Kippur’s extraordinary holiness still begins inside the ordinary cosmic cycle of evening and night.

L'Maan Tizkeru—“so that you may remember”—closes the tzitzit paragraph of the Shema (Numbers 15:40–41). It calls Israel to remember and perform the mitzvot, become holy, and remember the Exodus. On Kol Nidrei night, memory becomes active: remembrance should lead to changed conduct. The final Emet—“truth”—leads into the blessing of redemption.

Mi Chamocha draws from the **Song at the Sea**, Israel’s song after crossing the Red Sea (**Exodus 15:11**). “Who is like You among the mighty, O Lord?” celebrates God as incomparable in holiness and wondrous deeds. In the surrounding liturgy, the passage expands the Exodus memory into a declaration of divine kingship and redemption. Its central image is a people who have just escaped slavery recognizing that liberation reveals something fundamental about who God is.

“For on this day He shall make atonement for you, to cleanse you” comes from **Leviticus 16:30**, within the Torah’s description of the Day of Atonement. The verse links atonement with purification: wrongdoing is not only forgiven but cleansed, allowing moral and spiritual renewal. Its conclusion—“before the Lord you shall be clean”—makes Yom Kippur a direct encounter with God in which repentance aims not merely at pardon but at restored integrity.

The opening of the Amidah begins with **Psalm 51:17**—“O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare Your praise”—and moves into the first blessings of the standing prayer. It addresses God through the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, praises divine power over life and death, and declares God’s holiness. The opening establishes the Amidah’s basic posture: human beings can speak before God only by first asking God to make prayer possible.

The thanksgiving section of the Amidah acknowledges God as **the source of life, protection, and daily miracles**. It gives thanks for lives entrusted to God, souls held in divine care, wonders experienced continually, and goodness present “evening, morning, and noon.” Rather than focusing only on extraordinary miracles, the prayer treats ordinary existence as worthy of gratitude. Its central spiritual move is learning to recognize divine generosity in what might otherwise be taken for granted.

Ana B'Korenu, identified by de Sola Pool as a hymn by David ben Bekuda, introduces Selihot. Chanted responsively by reader and congregation, its recurring answers alternate “hear, O Lord” and “forgive, O Lord.” The hymn shifts the congregation into the penitential section and a mode of active pleading.

“Lord, hearken” begins the Selihot plea with verbs of urgency: hear, forgive, act, and do not delay. That language deliberately echoes Daniel 9:19, where the prophet pleads for Jerusalem and God’s people. On Kol Nidrei night, the prayer turns confession outward into petition: repentance is not only naming failure but asking for a response. Its repeated urgency gives the congregation a different posture from reflective prayer—the room is now pleading for mercy in real time.

Ashamnu is an **alphabetical communal confession** whose short Hebrew phrases name forms of wrongdoing from aleph through tav. It is spoken in the plural—“we have sinned”—even when individuals have committed different offenses, expressing collective moral responsibility. The confession avoids excuses and asks worshippers to name wrongdoing plainly. Its alphabetic structure suggests completeness: repentance requires examining the full range of behavior rather than isolating only the failures one finds easiest to acknowledge.

summaries.prayerAction: But in All -> We and Our Fathers
summaries.summary: This English confession insists that sin is not a problem belonging to someone else. Its repeated **“we”** places present worshippers alongside their ancestors in a continuous human pattern of failure. That can sound severe, but it also removes the illusion that repentance requires pretending to be uniquely righteous. On Yom Kippur, communal confession creates solidarity through moral honesty: everyone enters the liturgy as part of a flawed people still capable of return.

summaries.prayerAction: Yet Withal We -> Thee O Lord
summaries.summary: This passage refuses despair even after confession. The congregation acknowledges wrongdoing but still turns toward God, appealing to covenant, mercy, and the possibility of return. That movement is central to Yom Kippur theology: confession without hope would become self-condemnation, while hope without confession would become denial. The prayer holds both together. It allows worshippers to name failure honestly and still insist that relationship with God remains possible.

summaries.prayerAction: Of Us All -> Have Done Evil
summaries.summary: This communal reading broadens confession from individual acts to a collective moral diagnosis. Its force lies in the plural: **“we have done evil.”** Yom Kippur does not allow each worshipper to isolate only the sins personally committed and ignore the failures of the community one belongs to. The text creates a form of shared accountability without requiring everyone to be equally guilty of every offense. Confession becomes an act of belonging as much as an act of remorse.

Adir V'Naor is a recurring Yom Kippur piyyut built from an alphabetic series of divine titles and the refrain “Who is a God like unto Thee?” It leads into Micah 7:18–20 and appears across the day, linking Kol Nidrei, the morning service, and Ne'ilah with a shared penitential theme.

This reading introduces Micah 7:18–20, one of the Bible’s great statements of divine mercy: “Who is a God like You, pardoning iniquity?” The prophet imagines God **casting sins into the depths of the sea** and remaining faithful to the covenant with Abraham and Jacob. In Kol Nidrei Selihot, those verses provide the scriptural foundation beneath the surrounding piyyut. Mercy is not sentimental optimism; the service argues for it from the prophetic description of God’s own character.

summaries.prayerAction: Select Five Readers to Be Honored
summaries.summary: The service now assigns five readers for the five English psalms that follow: Psalms 1, 2, 3, 4, and 24. Giving each psalm to a different reader distributes participation near the close of Kol Nidrei and turns the sequence into a series of honored communal voices rather than one long reading. The psalms move through righteousness, divine sovereignty, danger, nighttime trust, and entry into God's presence, creating a compact reflective sequence before the concluding prayers.

Psalm 1, attributed to **King David**, contrasts two paths of life: the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked. The righteous person delights in God’s Torah and meditates on it continually, becoming like **“a tree planted by streams of water”** that bears fruit in season. The wicked are compared to chaff scattered by wind. The psalm concludes that God knows the way of the righteous, while the way of the wicked perishes (Psalm 1:1–6).

Psalm 2, attributed to **King David**, portrays nations rebelling against God and God’s anointed king. Earthly rulers imagine they can cast off divine authority, but the psalm answers with a vision of God’s sovereignty and the establishment of the king on Zion. It concludes by urging rulers to serve God with awe and seek refuge in the divine. The psalm combines political imagery with a theological claim: human power remains accountable to God (**Psalm 2:1–12**).

Psalm 3, attributed to **King David**, is linked by its heading to David’s flight from his son Absalom. Surrounded by enemies and told that God will not save him, David declares God to be **“a shield around me”** and the One who lifts his head. He can lie down, sleep, and awaken because God sustains him. The psalm turns danger into trust and ends by locating salvation and blessing in God rather than military strength (Psalm 3:1–9).

Psalm 4, attributed to **King David**, is an evening prayer moving from distress toward confidence. David asks God to answer him, challenges those who pursue falsehood, and urges reflection, restraint, and trust. The psalm contrasts anxiety over material prosperity with the deeper joy God places in the heart. It closes with one of Scripture’s clearest images of peaceful trust: **“In peace I will lie down and sleep”** because God alone provides security (Psalm 4:1–9).

Psalm 24, attributed to **King David**, begins by declaring that the earth and everything in it belong to God. It asks who may ascend God’s mountain and answers: one with **clean hands and a pure heart**. The final section imagines ancient gates opening to receive the “King of Glory,” identified as the mighty Lord of hosts. The psalm joins ethical character with divine kingship: approaching holiness requires both reverence and integrity (Psalm 24:1–10).

“May it be Your will” closes this block of readings by turning reflection into petition.
